newsitem.title: USA: FCC chief says BT-MCI deal should be cleared.
newsitem.headline: FCC chief says BT-MCI deal should be cleared.

text.p: The nation's top phone regulator said Monday his agency should approve British Telecommunication Plc's proposed $21 billion merger with MCI Communications Corp. after the carriers promised to take steps to ensure competition on the U.S.-British phone route.

Clearance by the Federal Communications Commission's four commissioners represents the last big regulatory hurdle for British Telecom and No. 2 U.S. long-distance carrier MCI, which announced their merger plans last November.
Analysts said FCC Chairman Reed Hundt's endorsement may be timed to give Washington-based MCI a shot in the arm a day ahead of a BT board of directors meeting planned for Tuesday.

Angry BT shareholders have called for a renegotiation of the deal's price tag after MCI revealed earlier this month it could lose up to $800 million this year because of red ink tied to entering the local phone business.

Hundt said in a statement that, based on commitments by the two carriers to give other companies a crack at the U.S.-British phone market, "I personally believe we can and should approve the BT-MCI merger as in the public interest."
In a separate interview, Commissioner Susan Ness called the BT-MCI pledges "very positive steps" but said she was not yet prepared to endorse the corporate marriage.

FCC officials said MCI promised to support efforts by the European Union to give British phone customers equal access to all long-distance carriers. British residents must now dial extra digits to use another carrier.
As a result, MCI could face much higher costs for completing calls to Britain if BT were to drag its feet on European requirements for equal access, agency officials said.

BT and MCI also promised to make available to competitors sufficient capacity on a key trans-Atlantic submarine cable between the United States and Britain. Both control a large chunk of the cable's capacity.
Underseas cable capacity has been clogged by increasing Internet traffic.

Hundt also cited BT's recent decision to sharply reduce the cost for completing overseas calls to the United Kingdom. The so-called settlement rate has fallen to 7 cents from 11 cents a minute, one of the lowest rates in the world.
And the British government recently agreed to sever all ownership ties with BT, providing added assurance that BT "would not enjoy any special advantages over other U.K. carriers," Hundt said.
MCI stock dropped 9.375 cents to $34.71875 on Nasdaq.
